rows.notes: The paper is a case report/policy synthesis built on an 'extensive and comprehensive literature review and data analysis' of secondary sources (WAPDA/SMO monitoring, Basharat et al. [3], Saeed et al. [1], Bastiaanssen [18]); it presents no own experiment, survey or model. Even if treated as primary, it contains nothing on drip or micro-irrigation: waterlogging and salinity reductions it discusses are attributed to reduced canal supplies during the 1999-2002 drought, increased groundwater pumping and drainage works (Sections 4.2, 5, Figures 8-10). Micro-irrigation appears only once, as a recommended water-saving technique to accompany curtailed surface supplies (Section 6.1), not as a studied intervention. The technology is a mismatch (surface-water reallocation/conjunctive management vs drip).

Same study as above: a literature-based case report with no own data on drip/micro-irrigation. It gives a provincial groundwater balance for Sindh (Table 4, from Halcrow-ACE [8]) showing recharge from canal seepage and irrigation return flows, and argues that reducing canal supplies would lower water tables, but it never examines micro-irrigation or its effect on groundwater recharge. Micro-irrigation is mentioned only as a recommendation (Section 6.1). Technology mismatch; no own evidence on the claimed reduction of recharge by drip.

notes: Full text appears complete. The paper is classed as a synthesis/case report (Section 3 states the method is literature review and secondary data analysis); authors' own contribution is interpretation and recommendations plus field photographs. No treatment of drip or micro-irrigation beyond a single recommendation, so neither claim is supported by the study's own findings.
